title: Big tones, black musicians' training and Louis Armstrong's embouchure
summary: Pillars stresses tone practice, says few black musicians were taught to play their horns correctly, and argues Armstrong used brute force.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Was this typical of the Southwest

It was somewhat typical, yes, uh-huh. But we always did try to tell the guys, just work on your tones, let's blow hard out, blow it out. And practice your tone, practice whole notes, hold those notes, hold them. And we'd get guys conscious of it and then they'd start doing it.

But, see, what happens in a lot of bands, if no one ever says anything about tone, the guys never paid any attention. Because, see, so few guys -- so few black musicians learned how to play their horns right.

In that era. It's a little different today, now. It's much different now than it was back during that time. You take Louis Armstrong. If Louis Armstrong had been able to learn to play trumpet right, Louis Armstrong never would have had his lip -- you know, that big thing on his lip right there? And Louis Armstrong would have been able to, with the muscles in his lips developed properly, he would have been able to hit anything just like that, without any effort. Effortless. But he used brutal force, and he was just physical. And the man just had it, he was determined to do it, and did it. In spite -- you know what I mean, of all of the handicaps.
